headline: Massachusetts Appeals Court upholds rejection of DCF worker's vaccine exemption
dek: The court said allowing a social worker to remain unvaccinated during the 2021 COVID-19 response would have created an undue hardship for the Department of Children and Families and the vulnerable people it served.
body: The Massachusetts Appeals Court has upheld a lower-court judgment against a former Department of Children and Families social worker who challenged the state’s rejection of his religious exemption from a COVID-19 vaccination requirement. In an opinion released Oct. 15, the court said the evidence supported the department’s conclusion that keeping Timothy Jangl in a job requiring extensive in-person contact while unvaccinated would have created an undue hardship for the agency and threatened public health. The [published opinion](https://masslegalresources.com/2026/10/15/jangl-v-secretary-of-the-executive-office-of-health-and-human-services-ac-25-p-168/) identifies the case as *Jangl v. Secretary of the Executive Office of Health and Human Services*, docket AC 25-P-168.

The dispute grew out of a policy adopted during the pandemic, not a new vaccination order announced this week. Then-Gov. Charlie Baker’s Executive Order 595, issued in August 2021, required executive-branch employees to be vaccinated as a condition of continued employment while directing agencies to create a process for limited religious accommodations. Jangl worked as a social worker in DCF’s Greenfield office. The court’s account says he served 19 families and regularly visited homes, supervised parenting time, attended court proceedings, accompanied children to appointments and handled emergency duties.

Jangl asked to reduce his office time and continue working remotely, while wearing a mask during client visits and undergoing weekly COVID-19 testing. DCF and the Executive Office of Health and Human Services denied the request after reviewing his duties and the department’s assessment that those measures would not provide protection comparable to vaccination. Jangl resigned in October 2021 rather than receive the vaccine. He later sued, alleging religious discrimination under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 151B, which requires employers to accommodate religious practice unless the accommodation would cause undue hardship.

The Appeals Court said Jangl’s beliefs could be treated as sincerely held, but that did not end the legal analysis. The court focused on the work he was expected to perform: close contact with children and families, including children with health vulnerabilities, plus emergency home visits. It also pointed to staffing shortages at DCF. In the court’s reasoning, an infection or outbreak could have impaired Jangl’s work, spread among families and co-workers, and reduced the department’s ability to deliver necessary social services. The judges concluded that the public-health and operational risks fit the statute’s definition of undue hardship and affirmed the judgment.

A second issue involved the evidence used to support the state’s position. Jangl argued that a medical affidavit should have been excluded because Dr. Lawrence Madoff, the state Department of Public Health’s infectious-disease medical director, had not personally conducted the research behind every study he cited. The court rejected that argument. It said Madoff’s board certifications in internal medicine and infectious diseases, UMass Chan Medical School professorship, infectious-disease credentials and leadership of the state’s vaccination program provided a sufficient basis for expert testimony.

The court also said Jangl had not preserved a challenge to the reliability of the expert’s methodology because he did not request a formal Daubert-Lanigan hearing. The opinion noted that he offered no competing expert evidence to counter Madoff’s affidavit. That procedural point mattered because the appeal was decided on the record developed in the lower court, rather than through a new trial about vaccine science or the general merits of vaccination.

Universal Hub reported that Suffolk Superior Court Judge Rosemary Connolly dismissed Jangl’s case in January 2025 before the appeal. Its [local report](https://www.universalhub.com/2026/court-declares-medical-director-state-bureau-infectious-disease-and) also described the Greenfield social-worker position and the alternatives Jangl proposed. The Appeals Court’s ruling does not dispute that religious accommodations must be considered; it explains why this particular accommodation was not required under the facts presented, where the employee’s duties involved vulnerable children, emergency response and substantial face-to-face work.

The immediate legal result is narrow but consequential for the parties: the judgment for the state remains in place, and the Appeals Court did not order reinstatement or a new accommodation process. The ruling also does not itself create a new vaccination mandate for Massachusetts workers. Instead, it applies the state’s religious-discrimination and undue-hardship framework to a former pandemic-era employment dispute and emphasizes that an agency may rely on documented risks to public health and essential operations when evaluating an exemption request.
author: NorthEast News Desk
